To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we introduce PixelPlayer, an unsupervised learning system for sound source localization and separation, that learns to ground sounds to pixels.

1) We introduce PixelPlayer which learns to separate the input sound into components that represent the sound from each image pixel, 2) PixelPlayer learns a joint model of sound and image by leveraging large amounts (millions) of unlabeled video data, and 3) PixelPlayer outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines on a newly collected sound separation dataset.

1) we propose a novel system for learning to ground sounds in images, 2) the system learns from unlabeled videos, 3) we collect a new dataset for this task, 4) we evaluate the performance of our system on source separation, and 5) we show that the system learns to ground sounds and separate sounds into components.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following questions. Can we learn to separate sound sources from unlabeled videos? Can we learn to associate sounds and image regions? Can we use the sound and vision to control the volume of each sound source independently?
the following question: can we learn to parse sound in the context of images, and if so, what are its implications?
the following questions: How do we separate sound into its component sources? What are the sources of sound? How do we localize the sources of sound
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PixelPlayer is a system that learns to separate sounds in videos.
we have shown the ability to separate sound sources in videos, and that this can be done without any additional manual supervision.
we have shown that we can separate sounds from images and that we can do this in a manner that is more efficient than previous approaches.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are the first to introduce a system that learns to separate sounds into a set sources from unlabeled videos.
we are learning a model to separate sounds from videos.
we learn to separate sounds in videos using a model trained on unlabeled video.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, by leveraging unlabeled data and a simple model, we can jointly learn to parse sounds and images.
, in the absence of labeled data, the visual and audio signals can be used to learn a joint model for sound separation and sound-to-pixel localization.
the sound of pixels is learnable from unlabeled videos.
